It is best understood simply as a term for weeping, without extending it to additional meanings not established by its recorded use.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the proper name “Baal Zebub.” It identifies a specific named figure rather than describing an ordinary action, quality, or object. The word occurs eight times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within four verses of 2 Kings 1. In those passages, it appears in speech and in statements connected with death, while remaining the object of the surrounding actions and words. Its exact significance in any individual verse depends on that verse’s surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “brutish.” It functions as a descriptive word for a person whose understanding or conduct is being characterized in that way. It occurs five times in the Old Testament, appearing in the Psalms and Proverbs. Because the individual verse texts and surrounding passages are not included here, the word’s precise emphasis in each occurrence must be determined from its immediate context, but its central description remains “brutish.”

This Hebrew word is the proper name “Admah,” referring to a place rather than describing an action or quality. It appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, and each occurrence is rendered “Admah.” The name is found in Genesis, Deuteronomy, and Hosea, showing that it remains a place-name across its uses. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Hebrew word refers to “cheese,” a food made from milk. It names a tangible food rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears once, at Job 10:10. The word’s precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical meaning is straightforward: cheese. It functions as a concrete food term.

This Hebrew word means “treasurers,” referring to people entrusted with managing or guarding a ruler’s wealth and stored resources. It is a noun describing an administrative office or responsibility, not an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only twice, both times in Daniel 3, where it identifies a recognized group of officials. Its precise role in either verse is understood from the surrounding list of officials and the broader passage.

This Hebrew verb means “overcome.” It describes one force prevailing against or pressing successfully upon another. In the Old Testament, it occurs three times, in two verses, so it is an uncommon word rather than a broad term used throughout many passages. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is overcoming an opposing person, force, or circumstance.

This Hebrew word refers to an action, but its precise ordinary meaning cannot be stated from the available lexical information. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 1 Samuel 6:12 and once in Job 6:5. The word’s identity is established, yet no gloss, short definition, or approved English meaning is available to explain what action it describes. e.t: This Hebrew word refers to grass or green growth—vegetation that covers the ground and appears fresh or tender. It is used of the plant life God brings forth at creation, of greenery affected by rain or drought, and of grass that quickly withers. The word occurs 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, consistently describing this kind of living ground vegetation rather than a person or abstract idea.

This Hebrew word means “mischief.” It names a troubling matter or result rather than describing a person, place, or action. In the Old Testament, it occurs three times: once in Isaiah 47:11 and twice in Ezekiel 7:26. These occurrences place the word among warnings and descriptions of distress, but the precise force of each use depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains mischief: a harmful trouble or difficulty that has entered a situation.

This Hebrew word refers to “brushwood,” meaning a mass of small branches or scrub wood. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 64:2. As a noun, it identifies the material being described rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself points to brushwood as a physical substance.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “refined.” It describes something treated with care so that refinement is its defining quality. The word occurs seven times in the Old Testament corpus, appearing in Chronicles, Job, Psalms, Isaiah, and Malachi. Its exact function may describe what has been refined or the refining process itself, so the surrounding sentence determines how the idea is expressed.

In Biblical Hebrew, חָדַל is a verb meaning “forbear.” It presents forbearance as an action or condition involving a person, group, or activity. The precise force is shaped by the sentence in which it appears, but its central idea concerns ceasing from or withholding an action. This verb occurs 59 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Zechariah. Its broad use includes situations involving people, work, conflict, and activity coming to an end or being held back.

“Aznoth” is a proper place-name, identifying a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs twice, both within Joshua 19:34, and the name appears as part of the place-name Aznoth Tabor. Its role is geographic identification, not a general word with a broad abstract meaning. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its particular role in that passage.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise ordinary meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. The word “Hor” is a Hebrew place-name, referring to a location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs four times, all within two verses in Numbers: 33:32 and 33:33. The name identifies a particular location in those passages. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise significance in each occurrence must be understood from the larger passage.

This Hebrew word expresses “love,” describing a strong inward regard or desire directed toward someone or something. It functions as a verb, showing what a person or God favors, values, or takes pleasure in. In the Old Testament, it can describe human longing, God’s choice of Israel, and delight. It is also used for decorative fillets in the tabernacle furnishings, where the same word points to something joined or attached. It occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament.

This Hebrew word expresses that a person or thing “are” in a stated condition or description. It functions as a linking verb, connecting the subject with what is said about it rather than naming an action by itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears four times, in Numbers, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding words, but its basic role is to state what the subject is or how the subject is described.

It identifies the same named location wherever it appears, rather than expressing an action, quality, or teaching. The word occurs seven times, from Genesis through Judges, and is associated with passages that command concerning it, give it to others, or mention it in speech. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Jedidah is a personal name. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object, so it functions as a name within the sentence. This Hebrew word appears once in the Old Testament corpus, in 2 Kings 22:1, and is rendered “Jedidah” in the available English versions. The precise relationship of the person named to the surrounding people depends on the verse text and context, but the word itself serves as an identifying name.

This Hebrew word is a personal name rather than a common word with a clear everyday definition. This Hebrew word is the name “Jemimah.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs only once, in Job 42:14. The available English rendering preserves the word as “Jemimah,” rather than translating it into an ordinary English concept. Thus, its primary meaning is its use as a personal name. Its particular significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself serves to identify the named individual.

This Hebrew word means “poured,” expressing the action of causing something to flow out. It describes an action, not a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Exodus 30:32, and its English rendering there is “poured.” Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is the act of pouring something out. This is the word’s only recorded occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament.

Ithra is a personal name, functioning as a person’s designation rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 17:25, and the English rendering is consistently “Ithra.” Because it is a name, its meaning here is primarily identification: it points to a particular individual. The surrounding verse is needed to explain that person’s role in the passage; the name itself does not describe that role.

This Hebrew word refers to “chains,” describing something that binds or restrains. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 68:6, so its normal lexical meaning is supported by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. As a noun-like word, it identifies the binding objects themselves. The precise force of the word in Psalm 68:6 depends on the verse and surrounding passage, which are not included here.

This Hebrew word means “cummin,” a small seed used as a spice. It names an agricultural seed rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Isaiah 28:25 and 28:27. The surrounding passage places cummin among other crops and seeds that are sown, harvested, and treated according to their proper use, helping establish its ordinary meaning as a cultivated seasoning seed.

Here, the word means “show”: it expresses an action of making something known or visible. It functions as an action word, describing what someone does rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Hebrew Bible represented here, it occurs once, at Isaiah 46:8. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely what is being shown in that occurrence.

This Hebrew word means “clothed.” It functions as a verb, describing someone as clothed or the act of clothing someone. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Daniel 5, and each occurrence is rendered “clothed.” The word therefore refers to clothing as an action or condition, while the exact role in a particular sentence depends on its surrounding context.

This Hebrew verb describes licking—using the tongue to take up liquid or touch something. It is rendered “licked” and occurs seven times in the Old Testament, in five verses. Its uses include the image of dogs licking blood and the account of men lapping water during Gideon’s selection of soldiers. The word therefore refers plainly to the physical action of licking, while the surrounding passage determines its particular significance.

This Hebrew word describes treading—being walked upon or pressed underfoot. It can also be rendered "trodden," emphasizing the condition produced by such action. In its three Old Testament occurrences, it appears in Isaiah and refers to ground or a place subjected to foot traffic or pressure. The central idea is physical trampling or treading down, rather than a person’s inner attitude or a separate spiritual quality. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context. The word is also connected with the description of Jerusalem’s bitter condition in Lamentations 1:4.

This Hebrew verb means “push.” It describes forcefully driving against someone or something, especially in physical contact. In the Old Testament, it is used for an ox striking or driving against people, and for people or nations pressing against others. The word can therefore describe direct, forceful action rather than a gentle movement. It occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages about animals, warfare, and symbolic acts.

Its single occurrence makes it a rare Hebrew term within the biblical record.

This Hebrew word refers to the group called “Naamites.” It is a group designation rather than a description of an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 26:40, and identifies people known by this name. Its basic meaning is therefore a designation for the Naamites; the surrounding verse is needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

This Hebrew word means “shaking,” describing movement marked by trembling or repeated motion. It functions as a word for the act or condition of shaking rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word therefore emphasizes active opposition rather than a neutral disagreement. Its use points to a concrete feature connected with water management rather than an abstract quality or action. The surrounding wording determines the precise role these sluices play in each passage, but the basic meaning remains a water-related channel or passage.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Numbers 26:49. The available English rendering preserves the designation as “Shillemites,” so its basic meaning is the name of this identified group; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role there.
